events.title: Sarai, childless, asks Abram to take Hagar
events.narrative_summary: Sarai has borne Abram no children and has an Egyptian maidservant, Hagar. She tells Abram the LORD has kept her from bearing and asks him to go in to Hagar so she may be built up through her; Abram listens.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 16:3 places the next act 'at the end of ten years' of Abram's dwelling in Canaan. He left Haran at 75 (12:4), so about 85 years from anchor.abraham_birth. 16:16 (Abram 86 at the birth) narrows the ten-year mark: the birth is nine months after the conception, so the proposal is placed at 85.4 years (offset 85.4 years, REGNAL_YEAR, margin 6 months) so that conception + 9 months falls at about 86.15 years, inside Abram's 87th year count of 86.0-87.0. Rashi, Ramban and Radak read the ten years as the period after which a childless wife may be set aside or a second wife taken, and Radak counts only years in Canaan. The proposal comes just before the giving in 16:3, so it takes the same date.
events.ancient_year_marker: At the end of ten years of Abram's dwelling in Canaan

events.title: Sarai gives Hagar to Abram as a wife
events.narrative_summary: Sarai takes Hagar the Egyptian, her maidservant, and gives her to her husband Abram to be his wife.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Follows the proposal directly (16:2 to 16:3, no gap marked): anchored on its END with no offset; margin one day for the time to arrange it. The ten-year mark in 16:3 is carried by the proposal event.
events.ancient_year_marker: At the end of ten years of Abram's dwelling in Canaan

events.title: Abram goes in to Hagar and she conceives
events.narrative_summary: Abram goes in to Hagar and she conceives.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: The text gives no interval after the giving; conception is placed right after it with a margin of two weeks. The birth event counts nine months from this start.

events.title: Hagar, seeing she is pregnant, looks down on Sarai
events.narrative_summary: When Hagar sees that she has conceived, her mistress becomes small in her eyes.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Hagar 'saw that she had conceived' (16:4), which takes weeks after conception. Offset one month from the END of the conception (the 'from X end' line must show about 1 month later), margin one month; the text gives no figure, so this is an estimate. Duration two weeks for a continuing attitude.

events.title: Sarai lays her wrong on Abram; he leaves Hagar in her hand
events.narrative_summary: Sarai tells Abram her wrong is on him, since she gave her maid into his bosom and is now despised; she calls on the LORD to judge between them. Abram answers that the maid is in her hand and she may do to her what is good in her eyes.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: A conversation that follows Hagar's contempt (16:4 to 16:5) with no marked gap: anchored on its END, duration half an hour, margin a week.

events.title: Sarai afflicts Hagar and she flees into the wilderness
events.narrative_summary: Sarai deals harshly with Hagar, and Hagar flees from her.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Follows Abram's answer (16:6), the afflicting being compressed into the margin of a week. The flight lasts until the angel finds her at the spring on the way to Shur (16:7): urim travel Hebron to Beer-lahai-roi, hurry mode, about 148 km by road at 5 km/h, elapsed about 2.5 days. Abram's residence (Mamre/Hebron) is an assumption from 13:18.

events.title: The angel of the LORD finds Hagar at a spring
events.narrative_summary: The angel of the LORD finds Hagar by a spring of water in the wilderness, on the way to Shur, and asks where she has come from and where she is going. She says she is fleeing from her mistress Sarai.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: The spring is where the flight ends (16:7), so the scene is anchored on the END of the flight; a short dialogue of ten minutes. The margin of a day covers the uncertain flight length.

events.title: The angel tells Hagar to return and submit
events.narrative_summary: The angel of the LORD tells Hagar to return to her mistress and humble herself under her hands.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: The angel's reply continues the dialogue directly (16:8 to 16:9, 'And the angel said'): anchored on the END of the encounter, no gap.

events.title: The angel promises Hagar a multitude and a son, Ishmael
events.narrative_summary: The angel says he will greatly multiply her offspring beyond counting. She is with child and will bear a son, to be named Ishmael because the LORD has heard her affliction; he will be a wild donkey of a man, his hand against all and all against him, dwelling before his brothers.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: A further speech of the angel in the same scene (16:10-12, each introduced by 'and the angel said'): anchored on the END of the command, no gap, five minutes.

events.title: Hagar names God 'the One who sees me' and the well is named
events.narrative_summary: Hagar calls the LORD who spoke to her 'You are a God who sees me', having seen the one who sees her. The well is therefore called Beer-lahai-roi, between Kadesh and Bered.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Her response follows the angel's words (16:13) with no marked gap: anchored on the END of the promises, ten minutes. The naming of the well (16:14) is a later note on a lasting name and shares the event.

events.title: Hagar bears Ishmael to Abram at eighty-six
events.narrative_summary: Hagar bears Abram a son, and Abram names him Ishmael. Abram was eighty-six years old when she bore him.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Nine months from the START of conception (the pregnancy), margin two months, REGNAL_YEAR from the age statement in 16:16. The conception falls at about 85.4 years from anchor.abraham_birth (the proposal was placed there for this reason), so the birth lands at about 86.15 years, within the 86.0-87.0 range of 'Abram was eighty-six'. I did not anchor a second time on the birth anchor.
events.ancient_year_marker: When Abram was eighty-six years old

causal_edges.causal_explanation: The angel's word that Hagar will bear a son called Ishmael (16:11) comes true when she bears Abram a son and he names him Ishmael (16:15).
When Hagar sees that she has conceived, her mistress is lightly esteemed in her eyes (16:4).
Sarai complains to Abram that she is despised in Hagar's eyes now that Hagar has conceived (16:5).
Abram puts Hagar in Sarai's hand, Sarai afflicts her and Hagar flees from her (16:6).
Once Hagar is Abram's wife he goes in to her and she conceives (16:3-4).
Abram listens to Sarai's voice, and she takes Hagar and gives her to him as a wife (16:2-3).

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably 'hail' (Hebrew barad), though the meaning of the place name is uncertain.
entities.summary_bio: A place named only to locate the well Beer-lahai-roi, which lies between Kadesh and Bered. Its exact site is unknown.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew mal'akh means messenger; 'angel of the LORD' is a messenger who speaks for, and in this chapter is identified with, the LORD.
entities.summary_bio: A messenger of the LORD who finds the fugitive Hagar at a spring on the way to Shur. He questions her, sends her back to Sarai, and promises her countless descendants and a son, Ishmael; Hagar then names the LORD who spoke to her.

components.evidence_explanation: Gen 16:15: Hagar bore Abram a son, and Abram named him Ishmael.
Gen 16:4: when she saw she had conceived, her mistress was lightly esteemed in her eyes.
Gen 16:10: the angel says he will multiply her seed so it cannot be numbered.
Gen 16:6: she fled from Sarai's presence; 16:8 she says she is fleeing. Ends when she bears the child to Abram (16:15), implying she returned.
Gen 16:3: Sarai gave Hagar to her husband Abram 'to be his wife'.
Gen 16:4 says she conceived; it lasts until she bears Ishmael in 16:15.
Gen 16:1 calls Hagar Sarai's Egyptian maidservant; 16:8 still calls her 'Sarai's maid'.

components.label_value: At the spring in the wilderness
components.evidence_explanation: Gen 16:7 places her at a spring on the way to Shur; 16:14 names it Beer-lahai-roi.

components.label_value: A wild donkey of a man, dwelling among his brothers
components.evidence_explanation: Gen 16:12 foretells his wild, hostile and independent character.
Gen 16:1 says Sarai bore Abram no children, and in 16:2 she says the LORD has restrained her from bearing.

systems.name: Appeal to the LORD as judge between parties
systems.ancient_near_east_context: A wronged party could call on the deity to arbitrate where no human court was at hand, as in 'may the LORD judge between me and you'; such an appeal carried the weight of an invoked oath.
rules_and_mechanics: The complainant names the wrong and the party responsible.
The deity is invoked to decide between the two.
The appeal puts the matter in the deity's hands and may force the other party to act.

systems.name: Surrogate motherhood through a maidservant
systems.ancient_near_east_context: In Mesopotamian and Nuzi-type contracts a childless wife could give her slave woman to her husband so that the child would count as hers; the maid remained under the wife's authority. The practice protected the wife's standing and the continuity of the household.
rules_and_mechanics: The wife initiates and gives her own maidservant to her husband.
The child born is reckoned as the wife's ('I will be built up from her').
The maid keeps her status under the wife's authority, which can make rivalry likely.
The husband agrees at the wife's request.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Abram names the son Hagar bore Ishmael.
system_instances.significance_note: Abram follows the name the angel gave Hagar, accepting the child as his own.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The angel of the LORD finds Hagar at a wilderness spring and asks where she came from and is going.
system_instances.significance_note: The first appearance of the angel of the LORD in Genesis: God seeks out a fugitive foreign slave.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The angel tells Hagar to go back to Sarai and submit to her.
system_instances.significance_note: Hagar's return keeps the child within Abram's household.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Sarai blames Abram for the wrong and asks the LORD to judge between them; Abram hands Hagar back to her power.
system_instances.significance_note: Turns the surrogate arrangement into open conflict and leads to Hagar's affliction and flight.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Sarai gives Hagar to Abram as a wife after ten years in Canaan; Hagar conceives.
system_instances.significance_note: A human attempt to gain the promised heir, which brings rivalry between Sarai and Hagar.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Hagar calls the LORD who spoke to her 'a God of seeing'; the well is later called Beer-lahai-roi.
system_instances.significance_note: The only person in the Bible to give God a name; it marks her recognition that God sees the afflicted.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Hagar is promised uncountable descendants, a son to be named Ishmael, and a wild, independent future for him.
system_instances.significance_note: God's promise to Hagar echoes the promises to Abram; the name Ishmael records that the LORD heard her affliction.

edges.description: Abram tells Sarai that Hagar is in her hand to treat as she sees fit.
Abram goes in to Hagar, and she conceives.
Abram names the son Hagar bore Ishmael.
The angel tells Hagar to return to her mistress and submit to her.
The angel promises to multiply Hagar's offspring beyond counting.
The angel asks Hagar where she has come from and where she is going.
Hagar bears a son to Abram.
Once pregnant, Hagar looks down on her mistress Sarai.
Hagar calls the LORD who spoke to her 'a God of seeing'.
Sarai tells Abram that the wrong done to her is on him and asks the LORD to judge between them.
Sarai treats Hagar harshly, and Hagar flees from her.
Sarai takes Hagar and gives her to Abram as a wife.
Sarai asks Abram to go in to her maid so that she may be built up through her.
The LORD has heard Hagar's affliction, which is why her son is to be called Ishmael.
